title: Trek a full loop of the Annapurna Circuit
description: The ACAP and TIMS permits together run about NPR 5,000 (~US$38) and cover every trail in the conservation area, including Poon Hill and ABC. Crossing Thorong La at 5,416m is the hard day - start well before dawn to beat the wind that picks up by mid-morning.

title: Watch sunrise over the Annapurnas from Poon Hill
description: The viewpoint tower fills up by 5:30am in peak season, so climb the last stretch from Ghorepani by headlamp to get a spot on the platform rather than the muddy overflow around it. Clearest between October and November, when the Dhaulagiri-to-Annapurna wall is free of haze.

title: Watch sunrise over the Annapurnas from Sarangkot
description: Taxis queue from 5am for the drive up from Pokhara; stay the night before at one of the hilltop guesthouses instead and you'll have the viewpoint before the tour buses arrive. It doubles as Nepal's main paragliding launch site once the morning haze burns off.

title: Witness the cremation ghats at Pashupatinath
description: Only Hindus may enter the main temple, but the terraces across the Bagmati River give a clear view of the open-air cremations below - go quietly and never point a camera at a grieving family. Sadhus posing for tips cluster near the entrance; agree a price before any photo.

title: Wander Bhaktapur's car-free Durbar Square
description: Bhaktapur charges its own entry fee separate from Kathmandu's Durbar Square, and the town banned cars from its old core, so pottery still dries in the same squares potters have used for centuries. Stay past 5pm once the day-trip buses leave and the square empties out.

title: Stand at the Buddha's birthplace marker in Lumbini
description: The Maya Devi Temple protects the exact nativity stone behind glass, and the monastic zone around it is a mile-long strip of Buddhist temples built by different nations in their own national style. Rent a bike rather than walk it in the summer heat.

title: Acclimatise a day in Namche Bazaar
description: Everest Base Camp trekkers take a mandatory rest day here at 3,440m to let their blood adjust - hike up to the Everest View Hotel rather than sitting still, since gentle movement acclimatises faster than bed rest. The Saturday market is when porters from lower villages restock the town.

title: Climb Gokyo Ri for a quieter view of Everest
description: The Gokyo valley sees a fraction of the Base Camp trail's traffic despite matching views of four 8,000m peaks from Gokyo Ri, plus a turquoise lake system sacred to Hindus and Buddhists alike. Cross the Cho La pass to link up with the main Base Camp trail if you want both.

title: Track wild tigers on safari in Bardia National Park
description: Bardia has a higher tiger-sighting rate than Chitwan simply because it gets a tenth of the visitors. Go on a jeep safari with a park-registered guide, then add a dugout canoe float on the Karnali River for gharial crocodiles and river dolphins.

title: Trek the restricted trans-Himalayan trails of Upper Mustang
description: A restricted-area permit (around US$500 for the first 10 days) caps numbers into this former forbidden kingdom, closed to outsiders until 1992. It sits in the Annapurna rain shadow, making it one of the few treks worth doing in the wet summer months when everywhere else is drenched.

title: Bathe at the sacred 108 waterspouts of Muktinath
description: Hindus and Buddhists both rank it among the holiest sites in the Himalaya, and pilgrims brave the icy spouts year-round. Most trekkers arrive over Thorong La from the Annapurna Circuit side rather than the short jeep track from Jomsom - the approach changes how the place feels.

title: Camp beside the turquoise water of Rara Lake
description: Nepal's largest lake sits inside its least-visited national park - reaching it means a flight to Talcha followed by a two-day walk, since no road goes further. Bring your own tent and food; the handful of teahouses fill fast in the short window before winter snow closes the trail.

title: Wander the car-free Newari hill town of Bandipur
description: Most Kathmandu-to-Pokhara buses barrel straight past the turnoff, missing a restored 18th-century trading town with unbroken Himalaya views and none of Pokhara's touts. Stay overnight in a converted merchant house to catch the ridgeline lit up at sunset.

title: Cross the courtyard of Punakha Dzong at the river confluence
description: Built at the meeting of the Pho Chhu and Mo Chhu rivers, this is the winter seat of Bhutan's chief abbot and the country's most photogenic dzong. Arrive by mid-morning for even light on the courtyard murals, and time a March visit for the lilac jacaranda against the whitewashed walls.

title: Count the 108 chortens at Dochula Pass
description: The 108 memorial chortens honour soldiers killed in a 2003 border operation, and on a clear winter morning the cafe behind them frames an unbroken line of eastern Himalayan peaks. Clouds usually roll in by early afternoon, so treat this as a breakfast stop, not a lunch one.

title: Watch black-necked cranes winter in the Phobjikha Valley
description: The valley's wetlands host one of the world's few migratory black-necked crane populations, revered in Bhutanese Buddhism, and locals bury their power lines to keep the birds safe. Walk the valley's nature trail clockwise in the morning so the sun stays at your back.

title: Drive the highest motorable pass in Bhutan at Chele La
description: At 3,988m this is the highest point in Bhutan reachable by road, with Jomolhari's summit visible on a clear day and prayer flags strung the length of the ridge. The short walk up the adjacent hill loses most of the tour groups within ten minutes.

title: Explore the recently opened Haa Valley
description: Haa only opened to foreign visitors in 2002 and still sees a fraction of Paro or Thimphu's traffic, with two ancient temples said to represent a wrathful deity's body parts. It remains Bhutan's least-populated dzongkhag, home to more army barracks than hotels.

title: Walk the ancestral seat of Bhutan's royal family at Trongsa Dzong
description: Every Bhutanese king has served as governor of Trongsa before taking the throne, and the dzong's watchtower museum traces the dynasty from this one fortress. It sits on the only east-west highway in the country, so most visitors pass through rather than plan a special trip - worth the detour anyway.

title: Ride the Kandy-to-Ella train over the Nine Arch Bridge
description: Cyclone Ditwah damaged the highland line in late 2025, so as of 2026 the scenic train now starts at Ambewela rather than Kandy - check current status before booking. Skip the crowded viewing platform and instead ride the early train to Badulla, then tuk-tuk back to walk the bridge itself once the tour groups have gone.

title: Climb to the painted caves of Dambulla
description: Five caves hold over 150 Buddha statues and ceiling murals painted continuously since the 1st century BC, the best-preserved cave temple complex in Sri Lanka. Climb in the cooler morning hours - the same golden rock face doubles as a lookout over the plains toward Sigiriya.

title: Cycle the ancient city ruins of Polonnaruwa
description: The compact ancient city is best covered by rented bicycle rather than car, with the Gal Vihara's four rock-cut Buddhas the highlight most tours rush past too fast. Go at opening time - by 10am the stone paths have no shade and the ruins get seriously hot.

title: Visit the sacred Bodhi tree at Anuradhapura
description: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, its sacred Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi tree was grown from a cutting of the original Bodhi tree in India and has been tended by an unbroken line of guardians for over 2,000 years. Dress code is strict - shoulders and knees covered, shoes off at every stupa.

title: Watch wild elephant herds in Udawalawe National Park
description: Udawalawe stays open when Yala closes for its annual monsoon break, and its open grassland habitat makes elephant sightings close to guaranteed rather than lucky. Take the first jeep slot at 6am, before the grass browns out and the midday heat pushes herds into tree cover.

title: Walk a working tea estate in Nuwara Eliya
description: Sri Lanka's hill capital sits at 1,868m and can drop to single digits at night, so pack a jacket few people think to bring to a tropical island. Walk a working estate like Pedro or Mackwoods for the full pluck-to-cup process rather than just the factory shop stop most tours default to.

title: Hike to World's End in Horton Plains
description: The cliff at World's End drops 870m, but cloud rolls in most days by 9-10am, so the 9km loop trail needs a pre-dawn start from the gate to catch it clear. Baker's Falls partway round is worth the detour even when the summit view is socked in.

title: Snorkel the coral gardens at Pigeon Island
description: The east coast runs on the opposite monsoon calendar to Galle and Mirissa, making this the season to pair with a south-coast trip for reef sharks and turtles in the park's shallow coral gardens. Go early - glass-bottom boat traffic crowds the reef by late morning.

title: Surf the point break at Arugam Bay
description: Sri Lanka's best right-hand point break runs from around April to October, when the west coast is in monsoon and this side of the island stays calm and offshore. Main Point gets crowded at peak swell; a few quieter breaks sit a short tuk-tuk ride further down the bay.

title: Explore the Tamil north from Jaffna
description: The Tamil north only fully reopened to independent travel after the civil war ended in 2009, and Nallur Kandaswamy Kovil's Dravidian architecture and a cuisine heavier on seafood and chilli than the south feel like a different country. The causeway out to Nagadeepa island is worth the extra half day if you have it.

title: Track endemic birds through Sinharaja Forest Reserve
description: Sri Lanka's last significant rainforest and a UNESCO World Heritage site holds more endemic birds and amphibians per square kilometre than anywhere else on the island. Hire a park-registered tracker - the leech socks sold at the entrance are not optional even in the driest months.

title: Raft the whitewater below Kitulgala
description: The Kelani River here was the set for The Bridge on the River Kwai, and now runs a full morning of grade 2-3 whitewater followed by waterfall jumping and cave exploring in the surrounding rainforest. It's a popular Kandy day trip, so book the morning slot to beat the afternoon rain that raises the river level.

title: Snorkel with whale sharks in South Ari Atoll
description: South Ari holds the only documented resident population of juvenile whale sharks in the world, so sightings run on 70-90% of trips in any given month rather than a narrow season. December to March adds calmer, clearer water and a decent chance of mantas on the same snorkel.

title: Watch the sea glow blue at Vaadhoo's bioluminescent beach
description: The blue glow is bioluminescent plankton disturbed by movement in the water, so wade in and kick rather than stand at the shoreline watching. Go on a new-moon night - a bright moon washes the glow out almost completely.

title: Picnic on a private Maldives sandbank
description: Sandbanks shrink or vanish entirely at high tide, so operators time trips to the tide chart, not the clock - ask before booking if you want hours on the sand rather than a rushed one. The November-to-April dry season also means calmer boat transfers out to them.

title: Surf the reef break at Pasta Point
description: One of the Maldives' best reef breaks sits beside a resort that has historically limited the wave to its own guests - check current access rules before planning a trip around it. The swell window runs roughly March to October, the opposite season to whale-shark high season, so pick a purpose for the trip.

title: Step inside the coral-carved Hukuru Miskiy
description: Built in 1656 from coral stone carved with Quranic calligraphy and old Maldivian script, it's easy to miss entirely on a capital stopover between airport and resort transfer. Modest dress is required and non-Muslims should ask permission before entering rather than assume it's open.

title: Dine underwater at the Ithaa restaurant
description: Five metres below the surface under a curved glass ceiling onto the reef, it was the world's first all-glass undersea restaurant when it opened in 2005 and still books out weeks ahead for sunset seatings. The tasting-menu price rivals a night's accommodation, so most visitors treat it as the one splurge of the trip.

title: Look out over the Banaue Rice Terraces
description: Batad gets the postcard fame, but the main Banaue viewpoints show the full 2,000-year-old amphitheatre carved by the Ifugao without machinery. Terraces run greenest just after the June planting and gold before the November harvest - a dry-season visit misses the colour entirely.

title: Spot wild tarsiers in the Corella sanctuary
description: The tarsiers here are wild, not caged, so guides walk small groups along a set path and stop you well before flash range - the animals are so light-sensitive that a camera flash can cause them fatal stress. Keep your voice down; a startled tarsier can jump hard enough between branches to hurt itself.

title: Swim the turquoise water of Kayangan Lake
description: Long marketed as the cleanest lake in Asia, it's reached by a steep staircase over a limestone ridge before the water opens out turquoise over a submerged forest. Entrance fees are paid in advance in Coron town to manage numbers - arrive by 7am to get the lake before the tour-boat flotillas.

title: Walk the walls of Intramuros
description: The walled city is free to wander, but Fort Santiago, San Agustin Church and Bahay Tsinoy each charge separately - a 350-peso Intramuros Passport covers five sites and never expires, worth it if you're doing more than one. A touristy calesa ride around the walls is still the easiest way to see the whole perimeter.

title: Paddle the enclosed lagoon at Sugba
description: A protected saltwater lagoon ringed by mangroves and limestone cliffs, it's usually paired with a full-day island-hopping trip rather than visited alone - bring reef shoes, since the entry point is a floating raft over shallow coral. Calmer outside the June-to-September typhoon season.

title: Cruise the Loboc River on a floating buffet
description: The floating restaurant cruise is squarely a tourist experience, buffet included, but the mid-river stop where local kids sing and dance for tips is the part visitors remember. Take an earlier slot - later cruises can queue for over an hour on busy weekends.

title: Ride a kalesa through colonial Vigan
description: Calle Crisologo's cobblestones and Spanish-Chinese mestizo townhouses have survived since the 16th century largely intact, making this the best-preserved colonial town in Southeast Asia. Go after dark once the day-tour buses have cleared out and the lanterns come on.

title: Frame the perfect cone of Mayon Volcano
description: The world's most symmetrical volcanic cone is also one of the Philippines' most active - check the current alert level before planning anything beyond the roadside viewpoints, since the permanent danger zone shifts with each eruption. The Cagsawa Ruins, a bell tower buried by an 1814 eruption, frame the cone in every postcard shot for a reason.

title: Climb the crater rim of Taal Volcano
description: This is a volcano inside a lake inside a larger volcanic caldera, and the island itself is frequently closed depending on alert level - check before booking the boat. When open, a 500-peso horse ride covers most of the climb to the crater rim, sulphur fumes and all.

title: Watch sunset over Boracay's White Beach
description: A 2018 six-month closure for sewage and overdevelopment reset the island's rules - expect a 300-peso environmental fee plus a 150-peso terminal fee on arrival, and a genuinely quieter strip than the pre-2018 party years. Station 1 has the widest, whitest sand; Station 2 has the restaurants and noise.

title: Camp above the clouds on Mount Pulag
description: The 'sea of clouds' summit view requires a medical certificate, a compulsory two-hour orientation at the visitor centre, and a DENR permit booked well ahead - the daily cap is 500 hikers split into groups of ten. No certificate, no entry, so sort it in Baguio before you head up.

title: Snorkel beside sea turtles at Apo Island
description: A community-run marine sanctuary since the 1980s turned this tiny island into one of the most reliable places on earth to snorkel beside green sea turtles without a boat chasing them down. Fins only, no gloves, and keep at least two metres back - rules the local guides enforce strictly.

title: Island-hop the Hundred Islands
description: Only three of the 124 limestone islands are developed for visitors, so a hired boat and a full day is the way to see more than the same two everyone else stops at. Low tide exposes sandbars connecting some islands on foot - ask your boatman which ones before committing to a route.

title: Summit the Philippines' highest peak on Mount Apo
description: The country's highest peak requires a registered guide and a climb permit arranged through the local tourism office, and the standard route takes two to three days up and down through mossy forest before the final scramble to the summit crater. The dry summer months give the clearest views before rain makes the trail treacherous.

title: Dive with thresher sharks off Malapascua Island
description: Monad Shoal off this small island is one of the only places divers can reliably see thresher sharks, which rise from deep water at dawn to get cleaned by smaller fish. Boats leave the beach around 5am to reach the shoal by first light - the sharks descend again once the sun is fully up.

title: Drive the rolling hills of Batanes
description: From June 2026 every visitor must pre-register online through the SMART Tourism system before arrival, and touring the rolling Ivatan hills means booking an LGU-accredited operator - one is waiting at the airport if you haven't arranged one. Go outside the June-to-November typhoon season, when Batanes is regularly cut off entirely by weather.

title: Cross the curved Langkawi Sky Bridge
description: A cable car climbs to Mat Cincang's summit before the curved 125m bridge swings out from a single pylon 100m above the jungle floor - one of the world's longest curved suspension bridges. Fast Lane tickets are worth the extra ringgit; the base queue for the cable car can run over an hour in school holidays.

title: Walk the canopy bridge in Taman Negara
description: One of the world's oldest rainforests, older than the Amazon, its main draw is a 530m canopy walkway strung between trees 40m up - not for anyone with a fear of swaying rope bridges. Night jungle walks and rapids-run river trips fill out a longer stay; go outside the October-to-February monsoon when trails flood.

title: Trace the layered colonial history of Melaka's old town
description: A UNESCO World Heritage-listed port city where Dutch, Portuguese, British and Peranakan influences stack on top of each other block by block, from the red Stadthuys square to the ruins of A Famosa fort. The trishaws decked out in flashing lights and loud speakers are tacky and completely worth doing once.

title: Eat your way down Jonker Street's weekend night market
description: Melaka's Peranakan food street only runs a full night market on Friday, Saturday and Sunday evenings - come on a weeknight and half the stalls won't be there. Chicken rice balls and cendol are the two things to eat before anything else on the street.

title: Trek to the jagged limestone spikes of the Mulu Pinnacles
description: Fifty-metre limestone blades erupt from the jungle halfway up Gunung Api, reached by a three-day return trek with a final scramble up ladders and roots - guides cancel the climb outright if it's been raining, since wet rock turns lethal. Long trousers are non-negotiable; the rock shreds bare skin.

title: Climb the pagoda at Kek Lok Si Temple
description: Malaysia's largest Buddhist temple complex climbs a hillside above Air Itam, topped by a seven-storey pagoda blending Chinese, Thai and Burmese styles and a 30m bronze Kuan Yin statue reached by incline lift. It lights up with thousands of lanterns for Chinese New Year - the best night of the year to visit, and the most crowded.

title: Ride the funicular up Penang Hill
description: One of the steepest funicular railways in the world climbs from George Town to a hilltop that sits several degrees cooler than the coast, colonial bungalows and all. Book the earliest slot to beat both the heat and the queues, since clear-visibility mornings sell out fast.

title: Spot proboscis monkeys in Bako National Park
description: A short boat ride from Kuching lands you in Malaysia's oldest national park, where proboscis monkeys with their oversized noses are spotted more reliably here than almost anywhere else in Borneo. Time the return boat around the tide - the jetty can be unreachable at low water.

title: Watch synchronised fireflies flash along the Selangor River
description: The Selangor River is one of only two places on earth where fireflies flash in mass synchrony across entire mangrove trees rather than randomly. Go on a moonless night between 8pm and 11pm for the brightest display, wear dark clothing, and arrange your return driver before boarding - taxis don't wait at the jetty.

title: Ride the cable car up to Genting Highlands
description: One of the fastest cable cars in Southeast Asia climbs from the valley floor to a hilltop resort of theme parks and casinos, permanently several degrees cooler than KL below. Skywalk and ride queues build fast on weekends; go on a weekday if you can.

title: Order white coffee in Ipoh's old town kopitiams
description: Tin-mining wealth built Ipoh's colonial shophouse core, now known nationwide for white coffee and beansprout chicken - order both at one of the old kopitiams rather than the newer cafes trading on the name. The street-art alleys off Concubine Lane are a five-minute walk from the food, not a separate trip.

title: Dive the reefs off Tioman Island
description: A rainforest-covered island ringed by reef, reachable only by ferry or seaplane, with diving that rivals the Perhentians but a fraction of the crowds. Monsoon closes most resorts and dive operators from November to February - check what's actually open before booking outside the main season.

title: Walk the riverfront promenade in Kuching
description: Sarawak's laid-back capital takes its name from the Malay word for cat, and cat statues and a museum lean into it, but the real draw is the riverfront promenade at dusk and a bowl of Sarawak laksa for breakfast. It's the standard gateway to Bako and Mulu rather than a destination in itself - budget a day either side.

title: Trek the rainforest of Endau-Rompin National Park
description: Peninsular Malaysia's second-largest rainforest reserve after Taman Negara gets only a trickle of visitors, with waterfalls and indigenous Orang Asli guides leading multi-day treks. Access requires a permit and registered guide arranged in advance - there's no showing up at the gate.

title: Walk the trails of the Night Safari after dark
description: The world's first nocturnal wildlife park puts around 2,500 animals on show after dark across four walking trails and a tram loop - book the tram first if you want to save your legs for the walking trails after. Arrive right at opening; the last-entry rush means the first hour is the calmest.

title: Watch the Rain Vortex fall inside Jewel Changi
description: The world's tallest indoor waterfall drops 40m through a glass dome inside the airport's own terminal, free to view from ground level with light shows after dark. Come around 10am for the softest light and the thinnest crowds - it's a transit-hall attraction, so it never fully empties.

title: Take in the skyline from Marina Bay Sands SkyPark
description: The 57th-floor observation deck is the only way to see the hotel's famous rooftop infinity pool without booking a room - the pool itself is for guests only. Go for sunset and stay through blue hour to catch the skyline lit up and the light show on the water below.

title: Walk down through the cooled dome of Cloud Forest
description: A 35m indoor mountain inside a cooled glass dome, wrapped in the world's tallest indoor waterfall and a walkway spiralling down through cloud-forest planting from five continents. It's genuinely cold in there - bring a layer, since the whole point is a controlled climate a world away from the humidity outside.

title: Walk the National Orchid Garden in Singapore Botanic Gardens
description: Singapore's only UNESCO World Heritage Site is free everywhere except the National Orchid Garden, home to more than a thousand orchid species and hybrids, several named after visiting heads of state. Go before 9am to have the swan lake and rain trees to yourself before the joggers and tour groups arrive.

title: Eat banana-leaf curry in Little India
description: Serangoon Road's spice shops, gold merchants and the ornate Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple make this the most sensory-dense few blocks in Singapore - go hungry, since the banana-leaf curry houses here rank among the city's best. Deepavali lighting in October or November turns the whole strip into a spectacle worth planning a trip around.

title: Cycle the kampong tracks of Pulau Ubin
description: A ten-minute bumboat ride from Changi Point drops you on the last piece of rural 1960s Singapore left standing - unpaved roads, kampong houses and wild boar wandering the tracks. Rent a bike at the jetty; the island is flat, the roads are rough for anything but bikes, and taxis don't exist here.

title: See the golden dome of the Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien Mosque
description: Completed in 1958 with a 52m golden dome and Italian marble columns, it floats a replica royal barge in the lagoon beside it and lights up gold after dark. Visiting hours for non-Muslims are limited to a few short windows a day outside prayer times - check the current schedule before you go, and dress modestly; head coverings are provided for women.

title: See the Sultan's coronation regalia at the Royal Regalia Museum
description: Free entry gets you the actual coronation chariot, crown and regalia of the Sultan of Brunei, one of the last absolute monarchs in the world - a level of access most countries would never allow this close. It's one of the better free museums in Southeast Asia and one of the least visited relative to what's inside.

title: Cruise the Brunei River for wild proboscis monkeys
description: Small boats leave the waterfront near Kampong Ayer in the late afternoon to follow the mangroves upriver, timed for when proboscis monkeys come down to feed at the water's edge. It's usually combined with a water-village tour, since the boatmen work both routes from the same jetty.

title: Climb Seongsan Ilchulbong for sunrise
description: The paid summit trail up this UNESCO tuff cone has seasonal opening hours and stops selling tickets an hour before closing, with the whole site shut the first Monday of each month - check before a pre-dawn trip. Walk up from the village on foot rather than driving; the car park and tour buses jam solid well before sunrise.

title: Hike the autumn colours of Seoraksan National Park
description: Korea's most dramatic mountain range turns red and gold for about two weeks each October, and accommodation within reach of the park sells out two to three months ahead of peak foliage. The cable car up to the old fortress site is the easy option; the Ulsanbawi rock scramble is the one locals actually rate.

title: Visit the Silla-era temple of Bulguksa
description: Built in 751 CE, it's one of the finest surviving examples of Silla-era Buddhist architecture and a joint UNESCO listing with the cave hermitage of Seokguram further up the hill - a shuttle bus links the two, so visit both in one trip. Go early; the stone bridges and pagodas are the most photographed spot in Gyeongju by mid-morning.

title: Stay overnight in a Buddhist templestay at Woljeongsa
description: An overnight templestay here runs through a 3am wake-up bell, monastic meals eaten in silence, and a barefoot walk through the fir forest to the temple's nine-storey stone pagoda. Book direct through the temple's own templestay program rather than a general tour site for a more authentic, cheaper booking.

title: Swim at Haeundae Beach
description: Korea's most famous city beach gets packed shoulder to shoulder in August, when a beach-umbrella fee and strict no-swimming-outside-flag-hours rules both apply. Walk the coastal boardwalk to nearby Dongbaek Island at sunset once the crowds thin, rather than fighting for sand space at midday.

title: Wander the painted alleys of Gamcheon Culture Village
description: A hillside slum rebuilt as an open-air art project in 2009, its stacked pastel houses and mural-lined alleys are now one of the most photographed spots in Korea - and also still someone's actual neighbourhood, so keep noise down away from the main path. Pick up the stamp-tour map at the entrance; the site is a maze without it.

title: Watch the morning auction at Jagalchi Fish Market
description: Korea's largest seafood market has ajumma vendors selling everything from live octopus to whole tuna straight off the boats, with upstairs restaurants that will cook whatever you buy downstairs for a small fee. Go before 9am to see the actual auction, not just the retail stalls set up for tourists later in the day.

title: Cycle the tree-lined paths of Nami Island
description: A crescent-shaped island of tree-lined avenues made famous by a 2002 Korean drama, it still draws bus tours of fans decades later, especially when the metasequoia trees turn gold in autumn. Rent a bike at the ferry dock - the island loops in about an hour, and bikes make it more fun than a flat walk.

title: Watch the skyline light up from N Seoul Tower
description: The cable car or a steep uphill walk gets you to a tower covered in thousands of padlocks left by couples, with an observation deck that on a clear day reaches past the city limits to the mountains beyond. Go right before sunset to watch the city switch from daylight to its full neon skyline in one sitting.

title: Walk the terraced rows of Boseong's tea fields
description: Terraced tea rows curve over hillsides planted since the 1930s, and the plantation opens well before dawn for photographers chasing the low mist that settles between rows on cool mornings. Combine it with the nearby Damyang bamboo forest as a single day out from Suncheon or Gwangju.

title: Step into 600 years of history at Andong Hahoe Folk Village
description: A UNESCO-listed clan village still lived in by descendants of the Ryu family, its thatched and tiled houses sit on a bend in the Nakdong River exactly as they have for 600 years. The mask dance performance runs on a set weekend schedule rather than daily - check before you plan the trip around it.

title: Watch cranes winter over the reeds of Suncheon Bay
description: One of the world's five major coastal wetlands, its reed fields turn gold in autumn and its mudflats host hooded cranes wintering from Siberia. Climb Yongsan observatory for the postcard S-curve view of the reed channels - the ground-level boardwalk alone doesn't show the shape of the place.

title: Walk through the Manjanggul lava tube
description: One of the longest lava tube systems on earth, only about a kilometre of its 7km length is open to walk, ending at a 7.6m lava column formed when the magma level dropped mid-flow. It's a constant 11-12°C inside year-round, so bring a layer even in Jeju's summer heat.

title: Walk the full wall circuit of Hwaseong Fortress
description: Built in the 1790s using early cranes and pulley systems documented in a surviving construction manual, the 5.7km wall circuit can be walked in full or ridden by a small tourist train between gates. Climb to the Seojangdae command post for the view over the full fortress and Suwon beyond it.

title: Rent a hanbok in Jeonju Hanok Village
description: Nearly 800 traditional hanok houses packed into one old quarter make this Korea's best-preserved hanok district, and renting a hanbok for the afternoon from stalls at the entrance gets discounted or free entry to several sites inside. Come on a weekday - the main street is shoulder to shoulder with rented hanboks on weekends.

title: Ferry across Sun Moon Lake
description: Taiwan's largest lake runs an annual festival season from September to November with fireworks, a swimming carnival and a tea culture festival - check the calendar, since some events close the ferry piers for the day. The Xiangshan visitor centre platform gives the widest lake view without paying for a boat ticket.

title: Release a wish lantern at the Pingxi Sky Lantern Festival
description: The 2026 mass release dates are 27 February at Pingxi Junior School and 3 March at Shifen Square, with lanterns launched in waves every 20 minutes through 9pm - book a spot early, since the main field fills up hours before the first release. Outside festival dates you can still write and release your own lantern daily at Shifen, just without the synchronised mass display.

title: See the Jadeite Cabbage at the National Palace Museum
description: The collection here is what the Nationalist government carried out of mainland China in 1949, and it's so vast that only about 1% is on display at any time, rotated every few months. The Jadeite Cabbage and Meat-shaped Stone draw the longest queues - ask at the information desk which gallery has them before wandering in blind.

title: Ride the sunrise train on the Alishan Forest Railway
description: The Chushan sunrise branch line leaves Alishan Station in pre-dawn dark and climbs to 2,451m in time for sunrise over Yushan - tickets go on sale at the station office at 1pm the day before and sell out in minutes during summer weekends, October foliage and Lunar New Year. Buy your ticket the moment you arrive at Alishan, not the morning of.

title: See the Queen's Head rock at Yehliu Geopark
description: Wind and sea have carved a headland of mushroom rocks into shapes including the famous Queen's Head, which is visibly eroding and thinning at the neck each year - it won't look like this forever. Go on a weekday morning; the narrow rock walkways bottleneck badly under weekend tour-bus crowds.

title: Snorkel the reefs off Kenting National Park
description: Taiwan's southernmost tip mixes white-sand beaches with coral-reef snorkelling and a night market that runs later and rowdier than anywhere else on the island. Typhoon season, roughly July to September, can shut beaches with no notice - check conditions before locking in a multi-day stay.

title: Eat your way through Taiwan's oldest city, Tainan
description: Taiwan's oldest city and former capital has more temples per block than anywhere else on the island, and a street-food scene - milkfish porridge, coffin bread, danzai noodles - that locals rate above Taipei's. Shennong Street's converted shophouses are worth timing for evening, once the day-trippers from Kaohsiung have gone home.

title: Soak in a seaside hot spring on Green Island
description: A former political prison island turned dive destination, its clear water holds one of the only saltwater hot springs in the world where you can soak while watching sunrise over the Pacific. Ferries from Taitung cancel often in swell - build a spare day into the itinerary either side.

title: Bathe in the sulphur springs of Beitou
description: A short MRT ride from central Taipei, this is the easiest hot-spring town in Taiwan to reach without a car, with a public thermal valley too hot to bathe in and private bathhouses fed from the same source next door. Water here is genuinely sulphuric - leave jewellery at the hotel, since it tarnishes silver fast.

title: Stargaze from Taiwan's first Dark Sky Park at Hehuanshan
description: Taiwan's first certified Dark Sky Park sits above 3,000m with a purpose-built stargazing platform and close to zero light pollution - go around a new moon, since a full moon washes out all but the brightest stars. Temperatures drop below freezing at night even when Taipei is mild, so pack layers most tropical-island itineraries don't include.

title: Enter through the dragon at Kaohsiung's Lotus Pond
description: The Dragon and Tiger Pagodas are the postcard shot, but the rule here is tradition, not superstition-optional: enter through the dragon's mouth and exit through the tiger's for good luck, and doing it backwards is said to reverse it. The pond is at its best lit up after dark, when the pagodas and Spring and Autumn Pavilions reflect on the water.

title: Soak in the riverside hot springs of Wulai
description: An Atayal indigenous village turned hot-spring resort town, it pairs open-air riverside baths with a waterfall reached by a short cable car ride most visitors skip in favour of just soaking. Weekday visits avoid the queue for the popular public foot-bath section along the main street.
